items.claim: Where the template is evaluated decides the ceiling of the finding: a client-side injection buys arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, not code execution on the remote server, so the two must not be reported with the same severity.
items.body:
Where the template is evaluated decides the ceiling of the finding: a client-side injection buys arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, not code execution on the remote server, so the two must not be reported with the same severity.

HackTricks reference: Client Side Template Injection (CSTI) (pentesting-web/client-side-template-injection-csti.md)
items.disproof: A client-side template injection that yields code execution on the remote server, or that produces no JavaScript execution in the victim's browser at all, refutes this impact boundary.

sources.quote: The SSTI can allow you to execute code on the remote server, the CSTI could allow you to execute arbitrary JavaScript code in the victim's browser.
The vulnerability becomes exploitable when a developer allows user input to reach the expression engine directly. If this occurs, it indicates the developer is misusing the framework.

items.claim: The same template payloads used to prove server-side template injection are the right probe for the client-side case, because the client interpreter also expects a template and executes whatever it is handed; a field that renders template syntax as literal text is a clean negative.
items.body:
The same template payloads used to prove server-side template injection are the right probe for the client-side case, because the client interpreter also expects a template and executes whatever it is handed; a field that renders template syntax as literal text is a clean negative.

HackTricks reference: Client Side Template Injection (CSTI) (pentesting-web/client-side-template-injection-csti.md)
items.disproof: Template payloads that render as inert literal text in the client interpreter, or a server-side payload whose result differs from the client-side one on identical input, refutes the equivalence.

sources.quote: Testing for this vulnerability is very similar as in the case of SSTI, the interpreter expects a template and will execute it.
The vulnerability becomes exploitable when a developer allows user input to reach the expression engine directly. If this occurs, it indicates the developer is misusing the framework.

items.claim: An ordinary profile field such as a name parameter is the signal worth chasing, not an exotic input: any value that the server-side template engine renders back is a candidate injection point because the engine will interpret whatever the user put there.
items.body:
An ordinary profile field such as a name parameter is the signal worth chasing, not an exotic input: any value that the server-side template engine renders back is a candidate injection point because the engine will interpret whatever the user put there.

HackTricks reference: SSTI (Server Side Template Injection) (pentesting-web/ssti-server-side-template-injection/README.md)
items.disproof: A name parameter whose template metacharacters are stripped or escaped before rendering and come back as literal text, refutes it as an injection point.

sources.quote: This can potentially allow an attacker to inject malicious code into the name parameter, leading to server-side template injection.
It is possible to construct a relatively small template that renders to a very large amount of output, which could correspond to a high use of CPU or memory.

items.claim: With Jinja as the engine, it is the Jinja directives inside the injected template that turn template injection into code execution and control of the engine itself, so identifying the engine decides what the finding is worth.
items.body:
With Jinja as the engine, it is the Jinja directives inside the injected template that turn template injection into code execution and control of the engine itself, so identifying the engine decides what the finding is worth.

HackTricks reference: SSTI (Server Side Template Injection) (pentesting-web/ssti-server-side-template-injection/README.md)
items.disproof: Jinja syntax injected into a template that renders as literal text with no directive evaluated and no code execution, refutes this mechanism.

sources.quote: This payload can contain Jinja template directives that enable the attacker to execute unauthorized code or manipulate the template engine, potentially gaining control over the server.
It is possible to construct a relatively small template that renders to a very large amount of output, which could correspond to a high use of CPU or memory.

items.claim: The whole defence for server-side template injection sits at one boundary, the insertion of user input into the template, so that is the only place worth verifying rather than trusting escaping applied somewhere else in the flow.
items.body:

items.disproof: Template syntax surviving insertion into the template and being evaluated by the engine refutes sanitization and validation happening at that insertion point.

sources.quote: To prevent server-side template injection vulnerabilities, developers should ensure that user input is properly sanitized and validated before being inserted into templates.
